translations.intro.narration.arrival: Before Mid-Autumn, Osmanthus Street is hung full of lanterns. {player_name} just arrived at the street entrance and heard that the treasure of the lantern fair — the giant rabbit lantern — has flown away without wings.
translations.intro.line.granny_greeting: You are the detective who came to investigate the case? Good, good. That rabbit lantern was tied by my own hands, one bamboo one paper, and it accompanied the neighbours for forty Mid-Autumns. The thief who stole the lantern, I think, is a rabbit's tail — cannot be long!
translations.intro.line.kit_joke: Grandma, calm down! That rabbit is bigger than my car, who can steal it? Unless it escaped by itself and ran back to the moon to find Sister Chang'e to celebrate Mid-Autumn.
translations.intro.choice.follow: Follow the colourful paper pieces on the ground
translations.intro.choice.ask: Go to the tea restaurant to ask the boss
translations.intro.ending.a: The colourful paper pieces led all the way to the rooftop: the rabbit lantern sat there well, and the broken ear was patched with new paper. It turned out Ah Kit secretly moved it to repair, wanting to give Grandma a surprise.
translations.intro.ending.b: The tea restaurant boss said while wiping the cup: 「Rabbit? Just sat on Ah Kit's motorcycle and left, still wearing a helmet.」 You rushed out the door, only saw a rabbit head floating farther and farther in the traffic……

translations.intro.narration.arrival: It is the eve of the Mid-Autumn Festival and Kwai Heung Street is strung with lanterns. {player_name} has only just reached the corner when the news arrives: the fair's prize treasure, the giant rabbit lantern, has vanished without a trace.
translations.intro.line.granny_greeting: So you're the detective? Good, good. I made that rabbit lantern with my own hands, every bamboo strip and every scrap of paper, and it has kept the neighbours company for forty Mid-Autumns. The thief? A rabbit's tail, that one: it won't be long.
translations.intro.line.kit_joke: Calm down, Granny! That rabbit's bigger than my bike, who could even nick it? Unless it ran off by itself, back to the moon to spend the festival with Chang'e.
translations.intro.choice.follow: Follow the scraps of coloured paper
translations.intro.ending.a: The paper scraps lead all the way up to the rooftop, where the rabbit lantern sits safe and sound, a new patch of paper over its torn ear. It was Kit all along: he had carried it up here in secret to repair it as a surprise for Granny.
translations.intro.ending.b: The cha chaan teng owner keeps wiping a glass. 'The rabbit? It's just gone off on the back of Kit's motorbike, helmet and all.' You run out of the door and see a rabbit's head drifting away through the traffic……

notes.intro.ui.start: Single verb to fit the 12-character button.
notes.intro.line.granny_greeting: Kept the rabbit image from the saying.
notes.intro.line.kit_joke: 'Nick' gives Kit a casual British voice.

findings.issue: 'A rabbit's tail, that one: it won't be long' is still a half-literal 歇後語; 'it won't be long' even suggests the opposite (that something will happen soon).
findings.reasoning: The point of the saying is that the thief's luck will not last. English readers need the meaning, ideally with the rabbit image.
findings.suggestion: So you're the detective? Good, good. I made that rabbit lantern with my own hands, every bamboo strip and every scrap of paper, and it has kept the neighbours company for forty Mid-Autumns. As for the thief, he won't get far. A rabbit's tail is short, and so is a thief's luck.

findings.issue: 'tea restaurant' is a calque of 茶餐廳; the glossary asks for 'cha chaan teng', and Ending B already uses that term.
findings.reasoning: The calque means nothing to English speakers and the two strings now name the same place differently.
findings.suggestion: Ask the cha chaan teng owner

findings.issue: The Chinese ellipsis '……' has been kept at the end.
findings.reasoning: English uses '...' (or '…'); the double Chinese ellipsis looks like a font error in the game.
findings.suggestion: The cha chaan teng owner keeps wiping a glass. 'The rabbit? It's just gone off on the back of Kit's motorbike, helmet and all.' You run out of the door and see a rabbit's head drifting away through the traffic...

findings.issue: Kit's slang ('nick', 'bike') is too informal for game text.
findings.reasoning: Standard English is easier for all international players to understand.
findings.suggestion: Please calm down, Granny. The rabbit is larger than my motorbike, so who could possibly steal it? Unless it ran away by itself and returned to the moon to celebrate the festival with Chang'e.

findings.issue: 'Vanished without a trace' loses the playful image of 不翼而飛 ('flew off without wings'); rabbits cannot fly, which is the joke.
findings.reasoning: Keeping the image adds a little humour to the opening.
findings.suggestion: It is the eve of the Mid-Autumn Festival and Kwai Heung Street is strung with lanterns. {player_name} has only just reached the corner when the news arrives: the fair's prize treasure, the giant rabbit lantern, has flown off without any wings at all.

findings.issue: 'Investigate' is a bare command; a fuller label is friendlier.
findings.reasoning: Players should know exactly what the button does.

## Task
Translate from Traditional Chinese (Hong Kong Cantonese usage) into English.

## Your instructions (written by the localisation team)
Translate each string into natural, idiomatic English for players of a story-driven mystery game.
- Keep the meaning, tone and purpose of every string; never add plot information that is not in the source.
- Interface text must be short and clear; choices must read as actions the player can pick.
- Dialogue must sound like the character who speaks it.

- Use the note to explain any non-obvious choice in one short sentence.

## Settings chosen by the team
- Translation strategy 3/5: balanced — keep the meaning and function exact, but rephrase freely where a literal rendering would sound unnatural.
- Cultural adaptation 3/5: balanced — keep references that create the setting; adapt ones that would only confuse.
- Register and tone: match the register of each source string.
- Character voice strength 3/5: clear — each character should sound recognisably like their profile.
- Glossary: use the glossary target term unless it clearly does not fit; if you choose something else, say why in the note.

## Target English variant
British English (en-GB): use British spelling (colour, realise, centre, travelling), British vocabulary and British punctuation conventions.

## Glossary
- 兔仔燈 / 兔燈 → rabbit lantern (required). Note: The missing lantern. Keep the same term in every string.
- 桂香街 → Kwai Heung Street (required). Note: Invented street name in an old Kowloon neighbourhood. Use this romanisation in every mission; do not translate it as 'Osmanthus Street'.
- 中秋 / 中秋節 → Mid-Autumn Festival (required). Note: Do not alternate with 'Moon Festival'. 'Mid-Autumn' alone is fine in dialogue.
- 茶餐廳 → cha chaan teng (preferred). Note: Hong Kong-style diner. You may gloss or adapt it where space is tight; avoid the calque 'tea restaurant'.
- 嫦娥 → Chang'e (preferred). Note: The moon goddess; the Jade Rabbit lives with her on the moon. A short gloss such as 'the Moon Goddess' is acceptable.
- 街坊 → the neighbours / the neighbourhood (preferred). Note: Warm, community word; avoid 'residents'.

## Project memory (approved by the human director)
No rules yet.

## Scene context
Kwai Heung Street (桂香街), an invented old street in Kowloon with a Sham Shui Po / Yau Ma Tei feel, on the evening before the Mid-Autumn Festival. The neighbours are hanging lanterns for tomorrow's street lantern fair, but its centrepiece, a giant paper rabbit lantern made forty years ago by Granny Wong, has disappeared. The player, an amateur detective, arrives, meets Granny and the delivery rider Kit, and chooses between two leads.

## Characters
- granny_wong: 黃婆婆 (English name: Granny Wong). Profile: Seventy-eight years old. A retired 紮作 (paper-craft) master who has made lanterns on Kwai Heung Street for over fifty years. The giant rabbit lantern is her masterpiece and has hung at the street's lantern fair for forty Mid-Autumn Festivals. Voice: Measured, slightly old-fashioned written-style Chinese. Fond of 成語 (four-character idioms), 歇後語 (two-part allegorical sayings) and proverbs. Scolds as a way of showing love. Never uses slang or English words. In English she should sound like a proud, sharp-tongued grandmother: complete sentences, a little formal, proverb-flavoured, never 'cool'. Relationships: Treats Kit like a grandson who needs constant correcting, and is secretly very fond of him. Polite but testing towards the detective.
- kit: 阿杰 (English name: Kit). Profile: Seventeen years old. A food-delivery rider who zips round the neighbourhood on an electric motorbike. Grew up on Kwai Heung Street and runs errands for Granny Wong. Voice: Light Hong Kong colloquial colouring on mostly standard written Chinese: the occasional particle (啦, 㗎, 囉), a few slang words (走佬 'do a runner', 飆車 'speed', 爆滿 'swamped') and English code-mixing ('old school', 'feel').
